learning-management-system-691:
## Why

Marking a review-queue item `stale` is intended to prevent an old backlog from dominating the learner's day, but stale items sort to the head of pending queue reads. `_pending_queue_statement` in `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:266-278` sorts by `due_at` ascending before priority, while `mark_stale_queue_items` at `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:345-353` clamps priority without moving `due_at`.

Because stale items are selected only when `ReviewQueueItem.due_at < stale_before` (`src/lms/scheduling/service.py:337-344`), every stale item has an older `due_at` than every non-stale item. `build_review_queue_overview` takes the first `daily_cap` rows (`DEFAULT_DAILY_CAP = 25`, `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:36`; `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:433-437`), so a stale backlog crowds out fresh due-review items.

For example, 30 items overdue by more than 45 days and 10 fresh due-review items result in the capped overview containing only stale items. This is a current learner-surface break.

## Scope

Make stale marking de-prioritise items in the learner-visible queue read.

## Non-Goals

Do not add retire or re-engage workflows. Do not filter stale items out of the queue; they must remain completable through `src/lms/scheduling/repository.py:136`. Do not change `DEFAULT_STALE_AFTER_DAYS` or `DEFAULT_DAILY_CAP` at `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:36-38`. Lowering the priority clamp without changing sort precedence does not satisfy this issue.

- [ ] Add a leading stale-status sort key to `_pending_queue_statement` in `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:266-278`, such as a SQLAlchemy `case()` expression ranking `ReviewQueueItem.reason_code == "stale"` after non-stale items.
- [ ] Keep the existing `due_at.asc()`, `priority.desc()`, and `id` sort keys in their current relative order.
- [ ] Add `tests/scheduling/test_sustainability.py::test_stale_items_sort_behind_fresh_items` to seed stale and fresh pending items and assert `build_review_queue_overview` returns fresh items first.
- [ ] Add `tests/scheduling/test_sustainability.py::test_fresh_items_survive_a_stale_backlog` to assert fresh due-review items appear in a daily-capped overview with more stale items than `daily_cap`.

never moves `due_at`.

      .order_by(
          ReviewQueueItem.due_at.asc(),

      )

      item.reason_code = "stale"
      item.reason_explanation = (

          "or adjust the learning goal instead of forcing catch-up."
      )
      item.priority = min(item.priority, 0.3)

- `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:340-344` selects only items with
  `ReviewQueueItem.due_at < stale_before` where `stale_before = decision_now - timedelta(days=stale_after_days)`
  (`src/lms/scheduling/service.py:337`, default 45 days at `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:38`). So
  every stale item has, by construction, a strictly older `due_at` than every non-stale item.
- `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:433-437` — the learner-facing daily view takes the first
  `daily_cap` rows of that statement (`DEFAULT_DAILY_CAP = 25`, `src/lms/scheduling/service.py:36`):

      items = list(

              _pending_queue_statement(learner_id=learner_id).limit(scheduler_settings.daily_cap)
          )

The priority clamp cannot have any effect between a stale and a non-stale item, because priority is
only consulted when `due_at` ties, and a stale item's `due_at` is always strictly smaller.

days and 10 fresh due-review items. `mark_stale_queue_items` marks the 30 stale. The next call to

Make the stale marking actually de-prioritise items in the queue read that learners see.
